reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO
clinicalPearls: A tick-borne flaviviral haemorrhagic fever endemic to India, first recognised in the Kyasanur forest of Karnataka and now reported across several Western Ghats states
Transmitted mainly by Haemaphysalis ticks, with monkeys serving as amplifying hosts, so the disease clusters among forest workers, farmers, and people with rural forest exposure
Illness typically begins abruptly with high fever, severe headache, myalgia, and prostration, often with conjunctival injection and gastrointestinal symptoms
A haemorrhagic phase with bleeding from gums, nose, or gut and thrombocytopenia may develop, and a subset of patients experience a biphasic course with a later neurological phase
The second phase, after an afebrile interval, can bring meningoencephalitic features such as headache, tremor, and altered mentation
Laboratory clues include leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and raised transaminases; diagnosis is confirmed by RT-PCR early and serology later, handled with appropriate biosafety
Management is supportive; a vaccine has been used in endemic districts of Karnataka, and tick-bite avoidance is central to prevention
reference.pathophysiology: Kyasanur Forest disease virus is an RNA flavivirus transmitted to humans through the bite of infected hard ticks, with monkeys acting as amplifying hosts during epizootics. After inoculation the virus disseminates and infects multiple organs, producing viraemia with a systemic inflammatory response, increased vascular permeability, and haemorrhagic manifestations together with cytopenias and hepatic involvement. In some patients the virus involves the central nervous system during a second phase, producing meningoencephalitis.
additionalDifferentials: Scrub typhus and other rickettsial infections
Other viral encephalitides (for the neurological phase)
additionalInvestigations: RT-PCR for KFD viral RNA during the early viraemic phase
KFD-specific IgM and IgG serology in the later course
Full blood count, liver function, and coagulation studies to assess severity
CSF examination and neuroimaging if the neurological second phase is suspected
Exclusion of dengue, malaria, leptospirosis, and scrub typhus given the endemic overlap in India
redFlags: Mucosal or gastrointestinal bleeding with progressive thrombocytopenia
Return of fever with neurological features such as altered mentation, tremor, or meningism marking the second phase
Hypotension, dehydration, or signs of multi-organ involvement
Severe hepatic derangement or coagulopathy indicating a complicated course
reference.prognosis: Most patients recover with supportive care, though the illness can be severe with haemorrhagic and neurological complications and a meaningful case-fatality rate; the biphasic form with encephalitis tends to have a more protracted recovery.
pitfalls: Attributing a forest-exposed febrile patient's illness to dengue or malaria and missing KFD in an endemic Western Ghats setting
Interpreting the afebrile interval as recovery and discharging before the neurological second phase declares itself
Neglecting biosafety precautions when handling blood and specimens from a suspected haemorrhagic fever
Overlooking occupational and vaccination history in patients from endemic districts
management: Provide supportive care as there is no specific antiviral, with careful fluid and electrolyte balance and haemodynamic support
Manage haemorrhagic complications with transfusion of blood components such as platelets and fresh frozen plasma as bleeding or thrombocytopenia dictate
Monitor for the biphasic neurological phase and treat meningoencephalitis supportively, including seizure control
Apply infection-control and biosafety precautions when handling blood and clinical samples
Emphasise prevention through the KFD vaccine in endemic areas, tick-bite avoidance and use of repellents and protective clothing
Exclude and treat co-endemic mimics such as dengue, malaria, leptospirosis and scrub typhus
Escalate to intensive care for severe haemorrhage, shock or encephalitic deterioration
